blocks.text: From this it is abundantly clear that no name could more aptly have been given to mice, and specifically to field mice, than one taken from the laying waste of fields. Hence עכבר achbar properly means this. This is confirmed by the usage of the Arabs, for whom عكبر [ʿkbr] achbar is not just any mouse but a species of field mouse, namely the male aljarbuo, as we showed above ^{a)}. Accordingly, at Esa. LXVI, 17, for the Hebrew העכבר haachbar the Arabic has اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo, as though these two were nearly synonyms. And the very thing with which Isaiah there reproaches the Jews, that some of them ate swine's flesh and העכבר haachbar, suggests that עכבר is a field mouse, and indeed that اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo, which alone, the Arabs report, is eaten. For the μύωξος [myōxos], that is, the glis [dormouse], which Jerome understands here, is not [II, 433] reckoned by the Arabs among the mice ^{(6)}. I admit, indeed, that in the Hebrew History of the Second Temple, p. 241, where the inhabitants of Jerusalem, besieged by the Romans, are said to have eaten נבלות הכלבים ועכברים, the carcasses of dogs, and mice, house mice must necessarily be understood, since in a city so closely besieged field mice were not to be had. And in extreme famine whatever was available had to be accepted as food. But Isaiah is speaking of foods which the Jews of his time, rebels against God's law, chose for themselves of their own accord, compelled by no necessity. Moreover, there is no one who seeks out the house mouse as food when other foods are available. Therefore in Isaiah the mice that served as food were field mice, not house mice. The same point is supported by the fact that in the passage of Samuel we have cited, עכברים achbarim lay waste the fields of the Philistines. For that is characteristic of field mice. It is certain, however, that the later Hebrews take עכבר achbar for any mouse. And Moses himself may have used it so, taking the word in a broader sense. To show this, Jonathan paraphrases the Hebrew העכבר haachbar at Lev. XI, 29. thus: ועכברא אוכמא וסמוקא וחיורא, that is, the black, red and white achbar: which are the three colours of mice. Of these the white is very rare, yet not unknown to the Greeks. Aelian, History book 12, ch. 5, on the temple of Apollo Smintheus in Hamaxitus, a city of the Troad: Ὑπὸ δὲ τῷ βωμῷ φωλεύουσι λευκοὶ μῦες [Hypo de tō bōmō phōleuousi leukoi myes], White mice nest beneath the altar. These are thought the most lustful of all; hence the proverb, Μῦς λευκὸς, ἐπὶ τῶν ἀκρατῶν περὶ τὰ Ἀφροδίσια· [Mys leukos, epi tōn akratōn peri ta Aphrodisia] A white mouse, said of those who are most incontinent in matters of sex. See Suidas, and what Aelian cites from Philemon in History, book 12, chapter 10.
As to why the Law declares the mouse an unclean animal, besides the reasons that occur to anyone, these too are adduced: that it is useless and harmful, and a type of those who say,
We are mere numbers, born to consume the fruits of the earth.

In Cyril, Against Julian, book 9: γαλῆ καὶ μῦς γράφουσί πως ἐφ᾽ ἑαυτοῖς τὰ δειλὰ, καὶ ἄνανδρα, καὶ ψοφώδη τῶν κλεπτῶν γένη [galē kai mys graphousi pōs eph᾽ heautois ta deila, kai anandra, kai psophōdē tōn kleptōn genē], [col. 1020] the weasel and the mouse represent the timid, unwarlike and noisy kinds of [II, 434] thieves. Since noisy is here plainly beside the point, I maintain that for ψοφώδη [psophōdē] we should read ψοφοδεῆ [psophodeē], that is, frightened at every noise. This word is used by Lucian in the Scythian and by Plutarch in the book On Preserving Health; and the same author, in the book Utra anim., says of the chameleon: Ὑπὸ δέους ἄλλως τρέπεται, φύσει ψοφοδεὴς ὢν, καὶ δειλός· [Hypo deous allōs trepetai, physei psophodeēs ōn, kai deilos] From fear it changes into something else, being by nature fearful and timid. Hence in Hesychius ψοφοδεὴς [psophodeēs] is δειλὸς, κενοφόβος, ὁ καὶ τοὺς ψόφους καὶ τὰ ἐλάχιστα φοβούμενος [deilos, kenophobos, ho kai tous psophous kai ta elachista phoboumenos]. How well this suits the mouse the excellent Poet shows in the fable of the country mouse and the town mouse, Satire 6, book 2.
The crash of the doors shook both from their couches: in panic they ran through the whole room, and trembled the more, half-dead, as soon as the lofty house rang with Molossian hounds. — — — —

The Hebrews adduce another reason, namely that eating mouse flesh induces forgetfulness. The most learned Buxtorf proves this from Avoda Zera ch. 3 (where, however, I do not find it) and from Beth Iacob fol. 181, where to the question why the dog knows its master but the cat does not, the answer is given that cats are forgetful because they eat mice, whose flesh, indeed whose leavings, if eaten, disturb the brain and memory. From this the following conclusion is drawn: האוכל ממה שהעכבר אוכל משכח תלמודו האוכל עכבר עצמו לא כ״ש One who eats of what a mouse has eaten forgets his learning: how much more, then, one who eats the mouse itself?
